Oliver Twist. This is Charles Dickens's second novel, serialized from 1837 to 1839, and it remains a dark social commentary on poverty, child abuse, and the criminal economy of the streets. The novel follows Oliver Twist, an orphan born in a workhouse who is raised in misery. He becomes famous for asking for "more gruel," an act of desperation that leads to his being sold into a brutal apprenticeship. Fleeing his master, Oliver flees to London where he falls into the hands of Fagin, a criminal mastermind who runs a school for child pickpockets in the underworld of the city. Fagin trains Oliver and other children to steal, exploiting their poverty and desperation. The criminal depths of the city are embodied in Bill Sikes, a brutal thief and murderer whose violence drives the tragic momentum of the plot. Sikes dies in an iconic scene when he is killed by his own dog while trying to escape. At the center of the emotional tragedy is Nancy, a prostitute and Sikes's lover who takes pity on Oliver and tries to help him escape. Sikes punishes her rebellion with brutal violence, bludgeoning her to death in one of Dickens's most shocking scenes. This death marks the turning point in the novel. The plot climaxes with Oliver discovering his true parentage and legitimacy, a melodramatic resolution that contrasts sharply with the grim realism that dominates much of the narrative. The novel is notable for its vivid and detailed depiction of London's poorest quarters, the workhouse system, and the criminal economy that preyed on society's most vulnerable.
